title: Invariant volume forms and valuation-unit translation multipliers
statement: Let $R$ be a discrete valuation ring with uniformizer $\pi$, fraction field $E$, residue field $k$, and $T=\operatorname{Spec}R$ [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring, def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Products and fibres are scheme-theoretic base changes [def-pc-base-change]. Smooth and finite type have the meanings of [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]; separated means that the diagonal is a closed immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Write $R^{\mathrm{sh}}$ for a strict henselization at a geometric closed point and $E^{\mathrm{sh}}=\operatorname{Frac}(R^{\mathrm{sh}})$ [def-weil-geometric-point, def-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-limit]. A subset $C\subseteq X(E^{\mathrm{sh}})$ of a finite-type $E$-scheme is bounded if some finite affine cover $U_i=\operatorname{Spec}B_i$, finite $E$-algebra generating lists $b_{ij}$, decomposition $C=\bigcup_i C_i$ with $C_i\subseteq U_i(E^{\mathrm{sh}})$, and integers $c_i$ satisfy $v(b_{ij}(x))\geq c_i$ for $x\in C_i$, where $v(0)=+\infty$. Let $G/E$ be a smooth separated finite-type group scheme of dimension $d$ [def-sc-group-scheme]. There exists a nowhere vanishing left-invariant section $\omega$ of $\Omega^d_{G/E}$ [def-sc-relative-differential-sheaf, def-sc-sheaf-exterior-power], unique up to multiplication by $E^\times$. For this section there is a group-scheme character $\chi:G\to\mathbb G_{m,E}$, where $\mathbb G_m=\operatorname{Spec}E[t,t^{-1}]$, such that, for every extension field $F/E$ and $g\in G(F)$, $\ell_g^*\omega_F=\omega_F$ and $r_g^*\omega_F=\chi(g)\omega_F$, with $\ell_g(x)=gx$ and $r_g(x)=xg$. If $G(E^{\mathrm{sh}})$ is bounded, then $v(\chi(g))=0$ for all $g\in G(E^{\mathrm{sh}})$, and hence also for all $g\in G(E)$.

source.place: 4.2 Proposition 1, Corollary 3 and Propositions 4-5, printed pp.101-103 (PDF pp.107-109). No use of Remark 6 or its external references. Primary scan read at https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~kamenova/homepage_files/Bosch_Raynaud_Neron_Model_tc.pdf; local literature copy WANTED.

proof.text: Put $p:G\to\operatorname{Spec}E$ and $V=e^*\Omega^1_{G/E}$. By [lem-sfb-group-scheme-differentials-from-identity], $\Omega^1_{G/E}\cong p^*V$. Applying [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-differentials-free-rank-fibre-dimension] at the identity shows that $V$ has some finite dimension $n$. The same theorem at any $x\in G$, together with the displayed trivialization, gives $\dim_xG=n$: the free differential module there has rank $\dim_xG$, while $p^*V$ has rank $n$. These ranks agree by tensoring an isomorphism with the residue field. Thus $\dim G=n=d$. Explicitly, $\dim_xG\leq\dim G$ by restriction of chains to opens; conversely, a chain $Z_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq Z_r$ of irreducible closed subsets and $x\in Z_0$ restricts to a chain of the same length in every open neighbourhood of $x$. Indeed its intersection with each $Z_i$ is a nonempty open in $Z_i$ and cannot be contained in the proper closed subset $Z_{i-1}$. Hence $r\leq\dim_xG=n$. We specify the left-translation trivialization next; an arbitrary bundle trivialization need not give invariant sections.

source.place: BLR 4.2 Propositions 1-2 and Corollary 3; Stacks Tags 02G1 and 047I.

proof.text: Here is the specified isomorphism $A:p^*V\to\Omega^1_{G/E}$. On $G\times_EG$ with coordinates $(g,x)$, the map $a(g,x)=(g,g^{-1}x)$ is an automorphism over the first factor, inverse $(g,x)\mapsto(g,gx)$. The square with top map $a$, vertical first projections and bottom identity is cartesian: a compatible test map lifts uniquely by the displayed inverse of $a$. Apply [lem-trf-relative-differential-sheaf-base-change] first to the second projection base change of $G/E$, and then to this automorphism over $G$: the differential isomorphism has local rule $df\mapsto d(f(g^{-1}x))$, with $g$ held constant. Pull it back along the diagonal $x=g$. Its source becomes $p^*e^*\Omega^1_{G/E}$ and its target becomes $\Omega^1_{G/E}$, by the composition comparison for ordinary module pullback. This is $A$, and at a $T$-point $g$ it is $(d\ell_{g^{-1}})_g^*:V_T\to\Omega^1_{G_T/T}|_g$. The chain rule and functoriality here follow on local generators from $d(f^\sharp a)$ and the universal property of Kähler differentials; exterior pullbacks send wedges to the wedges of their images. These formulas also prove compatibility with arbitrary base change.

source.place: BLR 4.2 Proposition 1, universal-translation construction; Stacks Tag 01V0; left-translation version of Tag 047I.

proof.text: Choose a basis $v_1,\ldots,v_d$ of $V$ and put $\omega=A(v_1)\wedge\cdots\wedge A(v_d)$. It generates $\Omega^d_{G/E}$ everywhere: under $A$ it is the top wedge of a basis of the free module $\mathcal O_G\otimes_EV$. For any $T$-point $h$, the equality $\ell_{(hx)^{-1}}\ell_h=\ell_{x^{-1}}$ implies $(d\ell_h)_x^*A_{hx}=A_x$. Taking wedges proves $\ell_h^*\omega_T=\omega_T$. This is an identity for the universal pair $(h,x)$ and hence for every base change. Conversely, if $\eta$ is left-invariant, then $\eta|_g=A_g(\eta|_e)$, by applying invariance to $\ell_{g^{-1}}$. This determines $\eta$ from its identity value, also for arbitrary $T$-points. If $\eta$ is only assumed invariant under $\ell_g$ for field-valued points $g$, as in the statement, take $c\in E$ with $\eta|_e=c\,\omega|_e$ and apply this at every $x\in G$ to the canonical $\kappa(x)$-point: locally $\eta-c\,\omega=f\omega$ with $f(x)=0$ in $\kappa(x)$ at every point, so $f$ lies in every prime of each affine coordinate ring and is nilpotent. Since $G$ is smooth over $E$ it is reduced [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced], so $f=0$ and $\eta=c\,\omega$. The line $\bigwedge^dV$ has basis $v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_d$, so two nowhere vanishing invariant top forms differ by exactly one scalar in $E^\times$. For $d=0$ the empty wedge is $1$ and the same statements hold.

source.place: BLR 4.2 Proposition 1 and Corollary 3; uniqueness also recalled at the start of 4.3.

proof.text: Over $G\times_EG$ with coordinates $(x,g)$, use the second projection as base. Universal right translation $(x,g)\mapsto(xg,g)$ is an automorphism with inverse $(x,g)\mapsto(xg^{-1},g)$. Differential base change and its local rule give an isomorphism of the relative top differential line. Apply it to $\omega$, and restrict along the identity section $g\mapsto(e,g)$. Comparing with the basis $\omega_e$ defines an invertible regular function $u\in\Gamma(G,\mathcal O_G)^\times$; invertibility follows because both the translation and its differential have the displayed inverse. Affine-locally the map $E[t,t^{-1}]\to\mathcal O_G(U)$, $t\mapsto u|_U$, defines a morphism $U\to\mathbb G_{m,E}$. The restrictions agree since they send $t$ to the same function, so [lem-weil-pbc-scheme-morphism-gluing] gives $\chi:G\to\mathbb G_{m,E}$. This construction is over the parameter scheme $G$, not just over extension-field points.

source.place: BLR 4.2 Proposition 4, functorial scalar construction; right-translation convention instead of inner conjugation.

proof.text: Left and right translations commute, since $h(xg)=(hx)g$. Thus $r_g^*\omega_T$ is left-invariant, and its identity value is $u(g)\omega_e$ by the construction in Step 4. The uniqueness argument of Step 3 over $T$ yields $r_g^*\omega_T=u(g)\omega_T$. Since $r_{gh}=r_h\circ r_g$, pullback reverses composition and gives $r_{gh}^*\omega_T=u(h)u(g)\omega_T$. The generator $\omega_T$ can be cancelled, so $u(gh)=u(g)u(h)$ and $u(e)=1$. Apply these identities to the universal pair on $G\times_EG$ to obtain equality of scheme morphisms. Hence $\chi$ is a group-scheme character, and in particular gives the required formulas over every extension field $F/E$.

source.place: BLR 4.2 Proposition 4; the character here is the inverse of the character for int_g used in BLR.

proof.text: Take the affine cover, generators, subsets $C_i$ and integers $c_i$ witnessing boundedness of $C=G(E^{\mathrm{sh}})$. On $U_i=\operatorname{Spec}B_i$, the regular function $u$ is a polynomial $P_i(b_{i1},\ldots,b_{is_i})$ with coefficients in $E$. For a nonzero coefficient $a_{i\alpha}$ its monomial has valuation at least $v(a_{i\alpha})+|\alpha|c_i$ on $C_i$. The valuation inequality for a finite sum gives the minimum of these finitely many integers as a lower bound for $v(u(x))$ on $C_i$. Taking the minimum over the finite cover gives one integer $M$ such that $v(\chi(x))\geq M$ on $C$. Empty $C_i$ may be ignored, and a chart with an empty generator list uses constant polynomials. Thus no general theorem that morphisms preserve boundedness is being assumed.

source.place: BLR 4.2 Proposition 5, first sentence expanded using the boundedness definition in the item.

proof.text: For fixed $g\in G(E^{\mathrm{sh}})$ and every integer $n$, the power $g^n$ lies in this same group, and the character identity gives $v(\chi(g^n))=n\,v(\chi(g))$. This integer is at least $M$ for every $n\in\mathbb Z$. A nonzero integer $a=v(\chi(g))$ contradicts that bound by taking $n$ arbitrarily large with sign opposite to $a$. Hence $v(\chi(g))=0$. The valuation on $E^{\mathrm{sh}}$ restricts to that on $E$, so the conclusion also holds for every $E$-point.

source.place: BLR 4.2 Proposition 5, bounded-subgroup argument expanded; no use of Remark 6.
